Virtual Machine Manager adds support for newer Linux distributions, improves VM deployment/networking, console stability, authentication, and SCOM integration. Operations Manager gains OpenSSL 3.x distro support, Ubuntu 26 support, improved web console reliability, Linux monitoring, and admin-only PowerShell widget editing. Service Manager adds MSOLEDBSQL19 and Microsoft Graph API support. Orchestrator improves runbook parameter handling and updates its command-line wizard to 64-bit. Data Protection Manager enhances SQL encryption support, recovery reliability, console/PowerShell stability, and accessibility. You Get One Exchange Left: Rethinking Azure Commitments Before February 2027 Team Blog: FinOps Author: Madhura Amlekar Published: 09/20/2026 Summary: Starting February 1, 2027, Azure reservations for services covered by savings plans can no longer be exchanged, except for one final exchange on reservations bought before that date. New reservations bought afterward get no exchanges. Reservations still offer deeper discounts for stable workloads, while savings plans provide flexibility across regions and SKUs. Teams should clean up unused resources, avoid committing against messy environments, and use savings plans for changing workloads before moving settled workloads to reservations. Buying at business-unit level improves chargeback and avoids duplication. The key shift is sequencing: optimize first, then commit carefully. Now Available: Management Group–Scoped Savings Plan and Reservation Recommendations in Azure Team Blog: FinOps Author: Obinna_Nwokolo Published: 09/29/2026 Summary: Azure now offers savings plan and reservation recommendations, including P3, at the management group scope in the Azure Portal and via REST API. This lets organizations assess commitment opportunities across entire subscription hierarchies in one view. The feature supports aggregated purchasing power, governance-aligned decision-making, and reduced analysis overhead for FinOps and central IT teams. Recommendations analyze historical usage, model optimal commitments, and estimate savings versus pay-as-you-go pricing. Users can access them through Azure Portal purchasing experiences or relevant Savings Plan and Reservation Recommendations API endpoints. Microsoft and IBM bring enterprise-scale workload orchestration to Azure with IBM Spectrum Symphony Team Blog: Azure Compute Author: DanaCozmei Published: 09/30/2026 Summary: Microsoft and IBM announced the IBM Spectrum Symphony Provider Plugin for Microsoft Azure Compute Fleet, enabling enterprises to extend and burst Symphony-managed HPC, AI, and analytics workloads into Azure. The integration connects Symphony’s workload orchestration with Azure’s scalable compute capacity, dynamically provisioning and releasing VMs based on demand. It supports multiple VM families, Spot and pay-as-you-go instances, and workload-based infrastructure selection to improve performance, availability, and cost efficiency. The solution helps organizations with established Symphony environments handle peak demand and large-scale batch workloads without permanently overprovisioning infrastructure. Announcing General Availability of Azure Lasv5 and Laosv5 VMs Based on 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors Team Blog: Azure Compute Author: sarah-zhou Published: 09/29/2026 Summary: Microsoft announced general availability of Azure Lasv5 and Laosv5 local storage-optimized VMs powered by 5th Gen AMD EPYC “Turin” processors. Built for data-intensive workloads, they offer faster compute, expanded local NVMe SSD capacity, higher IOPS, and up to 200 Gbps networking. Compared with prior generations, Lasv5 provides up to 30.7 TB local storage and 9.6M read IOPS, while Laosv5 reaches 138 TB and 20.7M read IOPS. Both support encryption by default and remote disk options. Lasv5 is available in five regions; Laosv5 is available in East US. Automating Private Endpoint DNS Across Azure Tenants with Azure Policy and Azure Lighthouse Team Blog: Azure Infrastructure Author: abhilashasr Published: 09/17/2026 Summary: In multi-tenant Azure environments, application tenants can't update the central tenant's Private DNS zones when they create Private Endpoints. The article proposes an Azure-native alternative to custom sync services. A DeployIfNotExists Azure Policy creates the private DNS zone group, using a user-assigned managed identity. Azure Lighthouse delegates that identity only Private DNS Zone Contributor on a dedicated central DNS resource group. Terraform and GitHub Actions with OIDC federation automate the rollout without long-lived secrets. The authors stress that this is a proposed design, not an official reference architecture, and should go through security review and a proof of concept first. Expanding access to specialized GPU infrastructure through Dapple and Azure Team Blog: Azure Infrastructure Author: Trinidad_Salazar Published: 09/22/2026 Summary: Microsoft is expanding access to specialized, topology-aware GPU infrastructure through Dapple integrated with Azure. Modern AI workloads depend not just on compute, but on GPU proximity, InfiniBand fabrics, low-latency networking, storage design, and cluster topology. Dapple’s Private AI Cloud provides dedicated GPU clusters while preserving Azure governance, security, and operations. Azure Kubernetes Service acts as the workload control plane, while Dapple manages infrastructure topology, maintenance, recovery, and lifecycle events. The Dapple Operator bridges both layers, enabling enterprises to run large-scale training, fine-tuning, and inference on purpose-built AI infrastructure without creating a separate operational domain. Dell Managed PowerScale for Microsoft Azure is now generally available Team Blog: Azure Storage Author: AzureAndrewChen Published: 09/10/2026 Summary: Dell Managed PowerScale for Microsoft Azure is now generally available in the East US region. Developed by Microsoft and Dell, the Azure Native ISV Service lets customers provision and manage Dell PowerScale through the Azure portal, CLI, PowerShell, and Marketplace billing while Dell operates the infrastructure, upgrades, maintenance, and support. The service offers OneFS file capabilities, private VNet access, up to 8.4 PB in a single namespace, NFS/SMB/S3 support, replication, compression, deduplication, and tiering to Azure Blob Storage. It supports hybrid data architectures, disaster recovery, analytics, and data-intensive workloads. Accelerated AI & Analytics workload on Azure Blob Storage: Up to 25x faster List Blobs operations Team Blog: Azure Storage Author: wolfgangdesalvador Published: 09/03/2026 Summary: Azure Storage is previewing an optimized List Blobs capability that returns results in Apache Arrow format, improving listing speed by up to 25x and reducing client-side CPU use by up to 15x. Enabled through a simple header or updated SDK option, it preserves existing API behavior and strong consistency while remaining opt-in. rclone testing showed 100K-object listings dropping from 24 seconds to 1.1 seconds with Arrow and parallelism. The feature is available in preview across major Azure Blob SDKs and REST, supports flat namespace accounts, and encourages parallel listing strategies for best performance. Locking down PAWs internet access when GSA drops Team Blog: Core Infrastructure and Security Author: ChristianFriedel-Jain Published: 09/14/2026 Summary: The article explains how to make Microsoft Global Secure Access (GSA) “fail-close” for Privileged Access Workstations, since GSA currently fails open if its client, tunnels, or services stop. The authors propose an Intune-deployable defense-in-depth design: Windows Defender Firewall switches between Private and Public profiles based on GSA event logs, restricting internet access to essential Microsoft endpoints when GSA drops; and Intune custom compliance with Conditional Access blocks cloud access if GSA is missing or services are not running. Dynamic Keywords, scheduled tasks, scripts, firewall rules, and Defender hunting support deployment, maintenance, and monitoring. MDATP Linux agent latest release reporting Team Blog: Core Infrastructure and Security Author: edgarus71 Published: 09/01/2026 Summary: The article describes a PowerShell 7 automation that runs on Windows to identify the latest Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDATP) Linux packages available in Microsoft repositories. It checks RPM and APT metadata across RHEL, Rocky, Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Debian, and SLES for prod, insiders-slow, and insiders-fast channels. Results are exported to an Excel workbook with release details, source URLs, timestamps, status, and errors. The report supports operational release visibility, not endpoint inventory, compatibility validation, or deployment guidance. It includes setup, scheduling via Windows Task Scheduler, validation steps, risks, and timestamp clarification. Foundry IQ with D365F&O and Fabric IQ Team Blog: Azure Architecture Author: Sayanika Published: 09/18/2026 Summary: The article describes building a Microsoft Foundry agent for a retailer using Foundry IQ, Fabric IQ ontology, Web IQ, SharePoint policies, Azure AI Search, and D365 Finance & Operations via ERP MCP. The solution connects customer, store, product, sales event, procurement, inventory, policy, and external market data to answer cross-domain business questions. It helps identify procurement risks affecting promotions, recommend cities for marketing spend, validate country-specific campaign rules, assess supplier or market disruptions, and determine store/event performance. The approach enables proactive, AI-driven decisions by unifying operational, contextual, and real-time external insights. AI Agent ROI Framework Team Blog: Azure Architecture Author: Yagneswari Published: 09/10/2026 Summary: The article presents a practical framework for measuring and maximizing ROI from AI agents. It emphasizes selecting high-impact, measurable use cases; accounting for full costs including infrastructure, development, data, talent, and operations; and evaluating value beyond labor savings through productivity, financial impact, risk reduction, and strategic benefits. It recommends ROI, NPV, and sensitivity analysis for investment decisions, supported by governance models such as AI Centers of Excellence, AI FinOps, and GenAIOps. Continuous dashboards, adoption tracking, and maturity models help organizations optimize AI agents over time and treat AI as a measurable business asset. Azure Delivers Strong MLPerf Inference v6.1 Results with NVIDIA GB300 & GB200 Team Blog: Azure High Performance Computing (HPC) Author: Mark_Gitau Published: 09/16/2026 Summary: Azure reported strong MLPerf Inference v6.1 results for DeepSeek-R1 on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and GB200 NVL72 platforms. It submitted rack-scale and cross-rack benchmarks, including GB200 at 18 and 72 nodes and GB300 at 18 nodes. Azure achieved the top reported Interactive score on GB300 and top Server and Offline scores on GB200 at both scales. The results show Azure’s infrastructure can sustain high throughput across latency-sensitive and batch workloads, reflecting the strength of its full AI system stack, including compute, networking, memory, and serving software. Scaling AI Storage: Azure Managed Lustre excels in MLPerf Storage v3.0 Team Blog: Azure High Performance Computing (HPC) Author: wolfgangdesalvador Published: 09/02/2026 Summary: Azure Managed Lustre achieved leading MLPerf Storage v3.0 results among major hyperscalers for AI training and checkpointing. In CLOSED-division tests, it sustained high accelerator utilization across five service tiers and file systems from 40 TiB to 25 PiB, delivering hundreds of GiB/s over five hours. For checkpointing, it reached 642.2 GiB/s write throughput and 489.6 GiB/s recovery throughput across Llama3 model scales up to 1T. The results show Azure Managed Lustre can provide scalable, predictable POSIX storage for large AI workloads while helping reduce accelerator stalls and optimize performance, capacity, and cost. Why long-running tasks on Linux Batch pools can restart daily and how to prevent it Team Blog: Azure PaaS Author: Sithu Published: 09/01/2026 Summary: Long-running tasks on Azure Batch Ubuntu pools may restart daily because Ubuntu’s default unattended-upgrades job installs OS updates and can restart core services such as systemd. This also restarts the Batch node agent, causing Batch to treat the running task lease as lost and re-queue the task from the beginning. It is not a workload bug, Spot eviction, or Batch platform failure. You can confirm via systemd timers, apt logs, and node agent journal logs. To prevent this, disable apt daily timers using a pool start task or custom image, while managing security updates through planned maintenance. Troubleshooting Azure Storage Deletion: Immutability, WORM, and Version Retention Team Blog: Azure PaaS Author: carlosbermudezlopez Published: 09/24/2026 Summary: Azure Storage accounts can become undeletable when immutable storage, WORM retention, legal holds, or version-level immutability protect underlying blobs. Even “empty” containers may contain hidden blob versions, snapshots, or soft-deleted objects that block deletion. Unlocked policies can be removed or changed, but locked policies cannot be bypassed until retention expires. ImmutableStorageWithVersioning cannot be disabled once enabled, and all protected versions must be cleaned up. Reducing version retention triggers Lifecycle Management rules, but cleanup is asynchronous and may take 24–48+ hours. Deletion must follow the order: blobs and versions, containers, then storage account. What’s new in Azure Firewall: Recent innovations Team Blog: Azure Networking Author: devanshirastogi Published: 09/04/2026 Summary: Azure Firewall has introduced five key enhancements to support modern cloud networking. Explicit proxy is now generally available, enabling centralized HTTP/HTTPS egress control without separate proxy infrastructure. IPv6 support is in public preview, helping organizations secure dual-stack and hybrid environments. HTTP header insertion is generally available for enforcing tenant restrictions, compliance, and downstream access controls. Auto-learn SNAT routes is generally available, reducing manual No-SNAT configuration by learning routes via Azure Route Server. Azure Firewall Premium also gains IDPS performance improvements, supporting higher throughput for TLS inspection, Deny mode, and high-bandwidth enterprise workloads. Adding network intelligence into a network-ready Azure migration plan Team Blog: Azure Networking Author: Sudha_Mahajan Published: 09/09/2026 Summary: Azure Migrate is adding Network Planning to make VMware lift-and-shift migrations network-aware. The feature helps teams discover and validate source network resources, map dependencies, assess readiness, recommend Azure networking approaches such as hub-and-spoke, NSGs, Azure Firewall, load balancing, and WAF, and include network costs in business cases. It aims to reduce migration risk by connecting application, security, networking, and migration stakeholders around shared evidence. The preview focuses on practical lift-and-shift planning, not advanced modernization or automation, helping customers and partners build more complete, costed, network-ready migration plans. Microsoft Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid is now generally available Team Blog: Azure Virtual Desktop Author: Steve_Downs Published: 09/01/2026 Summary: Microsoft announced general availability of Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid, enabling organizations to run Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts on-premises or at the edge using existing hardware and hypervisors such as VMware vSphere, Nutanix AHV, and Hyper-V. Connected through Azure Arc, session hosts are managed from Azure while desktops and apps are delivered via the Azure Virtual Desktop cloud service over outbound HTTPS. The offering supports phased cloud migration, compliance and cost constraints, and existing infrastructure investments. It uses per-user pricing, with infrastructure costs remaining on-premises. Microsoft also highlights partner support and Windows 365 Reserve for resilience. Now generally available: Regional resiliency for Azure Virtual Desktop Team Blog: Azure Virtual Desktop Author: Vidya_Iyer Published: 09/30/2026 Summary: Microsoft announced general availability of regional host pools for Azure Virtual Desktop in East US 2 and Central US. This new deployment type stores host pool metadata in the selected Azure region, reducing cross-region dependencies and improving resiliency by containing outages to a single region. Regional host pools preserve local replicas and paired-region failover where applicable. They can be created via Azure portal or PowerShell and must be used with regional workspaces, app groups, and App Attach packages. Microsoft recommends using regional host pools for new deployments in supported regions, with migration support for existing host pools coming later. Generally Available: Certificate Management for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes Team Blog: Azure Arc Author: NicolasMondada Published: 09/01/2026 Summary: Microsoft has announced general availability of Certificate Management for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes. The new Microsoft-supported Arc extension bundles cert-manager and trust-manager to automate TLS certificate issuance, renewal, rotation, and trusted CA distribution across edge Kubernetes fleets. It supports self-signed CAs for development and enterprise CA issuers for production, reducing operational overhead and security risk. GA adds production support, offline functionality during Azure disconnection, broad regional and Kubernetes distribution coverage, and ARM64 support. Existing preview users can update to the latest version without configuration changes. Episode 2: Reduce restarts with Hotpatch for Windows Server 2025 | The Azure Arc Check-In Team Blog: Azure Arc Author: Mason_Torres Published: 09/30/2026 Summary: Hotpatch for Azure Arc-enabled Windows Server 2025 helps reduce restart-driven maintenance by applying eligible security updates in memory without rebooting. It is available at no extra charge for qualifying Standard or Datacenter servers connected to Azure Arc and meeting prerequisites such as VBS/Virtual Secure Mode, UEFI Secure Boot, supported builds, and GA releases. Enrollment is done through the Azure portal, but updates are still managed separately through tools like Windows Update or Azure Update Manager. Hotpatch does not eliminate restarts: quarterly baseline updates, unplanned baselines, and non-Hotpatch updates such as .NET, drivers, and firmware may still require rebooting. Microsoft Intune Settings Catalog updated to support Windows 11, version 26H2 Team Blog: Intune Customer Success Author: Intune_Support_Team Published: 09/29/2026 Summary: Microsoft Intune now supports Windows 11, version 26H2 in the Settings Catalog, including day-zero support for validated Windows policy settings and updates to existing settings. New manageable areas include lock screen audio, MSIX allowed zones, password policies, printer driver ranking, privacy controls, and Windows Update pause/group policy settings. Administrators can configure these via the Intune admin center and should review, test, confirm compatibility, and monitor deployments. The Windows 11 26H2 security baseline is also now available, adding updated recommendations for printer driver ranking, TLS encryption support, and future NetBIOS settings. Moving from Windows Autopilot to Windows Autopilot device preparation Team Blog: Intune Customer Success Author: Intune_Support_Team Published: 09/16/2026 Summary: Microsoft recommends moving eligible user-driven Windows 11 Microsoft Entra join deployments from Windows Autopilot to Windows Autopilot device preparation. The new model simplifies provisioning through unified device preparation policies, enrollment time grouping, clearer OOBE progress, and better reporting. Organizations should transition in phases, keeping unsupported scenarios—like pre-provisioning, self-deploying, hybrid join, and co-management—on Windows Autopilot. The article outlines an eight-step migration approach: define eligible populations, design groups, map policies, assess device association, pilot, expand in waves, and retire old flows only after validation. Existing devices can be pre-associated without disruption until their next reset. Automating Compliance Scope Enforcement with Azure Policy Team Blog: Azure Governance and Management Author: gurjsing Published: 09/01/2026 Summary: The article explains how to enforce Azure compliance scope using Azure Policy, using Microsoft’s C5 certification as an example. It stresses that certifications cover only specific Azure services, not the whole platform, and customers remain responsible for implementation controls. The proposed process identifies the authoritative compliance document, extracts service-scope data into JSON/CSV, chooses allow-list or deny-list enforcement, maps services to ARM resource types, and deploys parameterized Azure Policy rules. Automation via GitHub workflows keeps scope data current, opens reviewed pull requests, and redeploys approved policy updates, turning compliance into repeatable “compliance as code.” Public Preview Annoucement: Azure Policy Custom Policy Versioning! Team Blog: Azure Governance and Management Author: stevenbucher Published: 09/14/2026 Summary: Azure Policy custom policy versioning is now in public preview, allowing custom definitions and initiatives to store multiple versions under one definition ID. Existing policies are backfilled to version 1.0.0. Users can create higher versions, pin assignments to major or minor versions, roll back by changing assignment references, and view version history and compliance by version. Versioning is supported in the portal, CLI, PowerShell, and REST APIs. Patch pinning is not supported, and preview limits each custom definition or initiative to four versions. Resource Provider modes and custom version overrides are not yet supported. This Cybersecurity Awareness Month, build skills to secure the future Team Blog: Microsoft Learn Author: philevans Published: 09/29/2026 Summary: Microsoft is marking Cybersecurity Awareness Month with role-based learning, events, challenges, and credentials to help people build practical security skills for an AI-powered future. Offerings include curated playlists for security, IT, developer, data, business, executive, and student audiences; the Defend the Tenant Challenge in a Microsoft 365 environment; and Cyber Genius hands-on training with Microsoft security tools. Participants can also watch “Ask a Cybersecurity Pro,” attend free global events, join the Microsoft Cybersecurity Pros community, and pursue Applied Skills or certifications to strengthen security habits, technical expertise, and organizational resilience. Skill vs. will: What leaders must solve for AI adoption Team Blog: Microsoft Learn Author: WilliamNations Published: 09/30/2026 Summary: AI adoption requires more than tool access and training. Leaders must diagnose whether barriers stem from skill gaps, employee willingness, or organizational systems. Research cited by Microsoft shows culture, manager support, and talent practices influence AI impact more than individual skill alone. Effective adoption starts with a priority workflow, role-based practice, clear responsible-use boundaries, manager modeling, aligned incentives, and outcome measurement. Hesitation may reflect unclear processes, weak governance, lack of psychological safety, or poor workflow design—not resistance. Leaders should remove system barriers and build practical capability tied to real business problems. Bring Azure AI to your private workloads on Azure VMware Solution Team Blog: Azure Migration and Modernization Author: rvandenbedem Published: 09/15/2026 Summary: The article explains how to make private Azure VMware Solution workloads accessible to Azure AI without moving data or re-platforming. It proposes using Azure AI Foundry managed agents connected through lightweight Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers running on VNet-integrated Azure Container Apps, with private ExpressRoute connectivity to VMware workloads. A SQL example shows read-only querying across two private databases using managed identity, Key Vault, and strict governance controls. The pattern can extend to file shares, APIs, NoSQL, and legacy systems, enabling secure, repeatable AI access to private enterprise data in place.

items.title: Locking down PAWs internet access when GSA drops
items.summary: By: Christian Friedel-Jain - Sr. Security Consultant | James Noyce - Sr. Security Solution Engineer Introduction Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) are among the most sensitive endpoints in any organization. A PAW, in most of our Microsoft consulting projects, exists to do one job safely: administer cloud services from a hardened device that is only ever allowed to reach a small, tightly controlled set of internet destinations. But an endpoint’s security posture is ultimately defined by its behavior under failure conditions. When we moved the internet access restriction for our PAW devices from a locally enforced restriction ( more about that later ) to a solution based on Microsoft Global Secure Access (GSA), we immediately identified a gap under failure conditions – but first a quick grounding on the moving parts. Global Secure Access ( What is Global Secure Access? ) is Microsoft’s umbrella term for Microsoft Entra Internet Access and Microsoft Entra Private Access — the components of Microsoft’s Security Service Edge solution. For a PAW device we are leveraging Microsoft Entra Internet Access as an identity centric secure web gateway solution to control exactly which internet destinations the workstation can reach, by applying a fine-grained set of rules and policies enforced through Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra. This configuration provides us better filtering capabilities, like web content filtering ( Global Secure Access web content filtering ) with TLS inspection (TLSi) ( Global Secure Access transport layer security inspection ) and additional features like Threat Intelligence ( Global Secure Access threat intelligence ), but it comes also with a downside. Currently by default, if the GSA client encounters an issue or cannot connect to its required GSA edge services, the GSA client will fall back to a fail-open state, rather than to a fail-close state. Difference between those two modes: Fail-Open: When a security or control mechanism fails, access is still allowed. Fail-Close: When the security or control mechanism fails, access is blocked. This blog post covers above problem and showcases a solution we built, as part of our projects, to achieve a “Fail-Close” state rather than having the current “Fail-Open” behavior. The enforcement of the “Fail-Close” solution we developed works at two independent layers, both are deployable through Microsoft Intune: A network layer: Windows Defender Firewall network profiles, a rule set with Windows Firewall Dynamic Keywords , and event-driven automation — restricts the device internet access in the moment GSA’s tunnels or services drop. An identity layer: an Intune custom compliance check paired with Conditional Access — denies the device access whenever the GSA client is missing or its services are not running. Together, they help to make sure a failure that slips past one layer is still caught by the other. From URL Lock Proxy to Global Secure Access Historically, we restricted internet access on PAW devices with the Windows Defender Firewall (for more details see here Microsoft Defender Firewall ) and a “URL Lock Proxy” approach (and here URL lock proxy ): an allow-list of permitted URLs that blocked every outbound HTTP(S) connection except the ones required for: Approved management portals, Authentication to Microsoft Entra ID, Management by Microsoft Intune, and Monitoring by Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. Previous internet access control via URL lock proxy. It worked, but it carried real limitations: No auditing of what was allowed or blocked, It did not scale and required a lot of wildcards to be used, A limited ruleset size — the size cap on the underlying registry key meant the solution simply could not grow, and It was not enterprise class. Microsoft Global Secure Access with its component Entra Internet Access replaces the URL Lock Proxy configuration entirely. We are using dedicated firewall rules for the GSA client, to allow the client to reach the Entra Internet Access edge service. Through Entra Condition Access, a GSA Internet Access traffic profile (security profile) is applied which blocks all internet access except the specific FQDNs needed for approved management portals/platforms, Entra ID authentication, Intune, and Defender for Endpoint. HTTP and HTTPS traffic is evaluated and filtered within the GSA Edge service itself, and a request to a destination that is not on the allow-list is blocked with a simple “ You can’t access this destination ” message. Additional features like filtering on URL level instead of FQDN, due to the use of TLSi, helped to remove most of the wildcards we had to use with the previous URL lock proxy approach. The result is: Access and the access results are auditable, More granular and centrally managed rule set, And genuinely enterprise class. PAW internet access control via Entra Global Secure Access Internet Access Result of blocked internet access The catch: Global Secure Access fails open GSA as the internet access restriction method is powerful, but it builds on the assumption that the GSA client is installed, running, and connected. When that assumption breaks, the client’s current behavior is to fail open. As a result, the device ends up with unrestricted internet access whenever: The GSA client is installed but cannot establish its tunnels with the GSA edge services (according to the Entra ID SLA this doesn’t happen that often – see Service Level Agreement performance for Microsoft Entra ID ), The GSA client on the PAW is installed but suspended, or Its services are disabled, or The GSA client component is not installed at all on the PAW device. Current fail open behavior in case GSA internet access is not available Left: normal operations - GSA internet access blocks access | Right: failure state - no filtering of internet access traffic On a regular end user device, the fail-open mode is a convenience. On a PAW it is exactly the wrong default: the very moment the protection drops away, the device becomes its most exposed. Therefore, we had to develop a solution to have a fail-close behavior. The Fail-Close approach The core idea is deliberately simple, and it uses capability that already exists on most of the Windows devices: the Windows Defender Firewall network profiles (more details here Windows Firewall Network Profiles ). Two of the available firewall profiles are repurposed to act as separate operating modes : Private profile: “unrestricted” HTTP(S). Internet access filtering is delegated to GSA Internet Access, so the firewall itself does not constrain destinations. Public profile: “restricted” HTTP(S). Outbound web traffic is limited to a mandatory set of FQDNs via Defender Dynamic Keywords and selected system processes — just enough for the device to stay managed and healthy. When the GSA client has successfully established its Internet access tunnel, the device is assigned the Private network profile. If GSA fails, the Windows Firewall profile is automatically switched to the Public network profile, restricting Internet access to essential destinations only. This profile transition implements the required fail-close behavior. Normal state — Private profile Normal state - Windows Firewall profile "private" doesn't perform internet access restrictions, GSA internet access performs filtering As soon as the GSA client is running, connected to the GSA edge services and has established the Internet Access tunnel (step 1), the client writes a success event to the GSA event log (step 2) (Internet Access tunnel connected — Event ID 142) When that event occurs, a scheduled task (step 3) runs a PowerShell script (step 4) that: Switches the device to the Private firewall network profile, Validates the state of all local GSA services, and Initiates an Intune custom compliance check (to perform additional validations). In case all validates were successfully passed, the PowerShell script enforces the Private firewall profile (step 5) and GSA Internet Access is being used to filter the internet access (step 6). Failure state — Public profile Failure state - Windows Firewall profile "public" enforces internet access restrictions The moment GSA stops protecting (step 1) the device, one of several failure events is written to the GSA event log (step 2) and triggers a different scheduled task (step 3) which runs a PowerShell script (step 4) that switches the device to the Public firewall network profile (step 5) and initiates an Intune custom compliance check, too. The failure signals we watch for are: Entra or Internet Access tunnel disconnected — Event ID 141 (logged roughly every 10 seconds while the tunnel is down), GSA services stopped — Event IDs 106, 206, 406, and 705, No internet connectivity — Event ID 638, and Services start initiated — Event ID 701. On the Public profile, the HTTP(S) outbound rule has Reusable Settings (Defender Dynamic Keywords - Windows Firewall Dynamic Keywords ) (step 6) assigned, which restricts the reachable FQDNs down to a mandatory set of endpoints. Additionally, mandatory applications and services are explicitly exempt from that restriction, so the device can still be managed, patched, and monitored even while it is locked down. Left: normal operations - GSA internet access blocks access | Right: failure state - internet access filtering by Windows Firewall Closing the gap when GSA is absent: custom compliance The firewall profile switch is event-driven — it reacts to the signals the GSA client writes to the event log. That works well for a device where the GSA client is present, but it leaves one blind spot: if the GSA client is not installed at all, or its services never start, there may be no events to react to. Those are exactly the scenarios where a device would otherwise fall back to unrestricted access, the solution uses a custom device compliance policy/check that does not depend on any event firing. It directly: Validates that the GSA client is installed on the device, and Checks the local GSA service state — confirming that the services are running, not just present. If either of those checks fails — GSA client is not installed, or its services are not running — Intune reports the device as non-compliant. Because a PAW’s access to cloud resources is gated by Conditional Access requiring a compliant device, a non-compliant PAW is denied access to the very cloud services it exists to manage. So even in the one case the event-driven firewall switch cannot see, access still fails closed — this time at the identity layer rather than the network layer. In addition, as soon as the local evaluation detected a non-compliant scenario, the custom compliance check flips the firewall profile to the Public profile, too. The profile-switching PowerShell scripts also initiate this compliance evaluation as they run in both the normal and failure states, so the device re-reports its posture promptly instead of waiting for the next routine Intune check-in. The result is defense in depth — two independent layers, neither relying on the other: Enforcement layer Mechanism What it catches Network Defender Firewall profile switch, driven by GSA event IDs (141, 106, 206, 406, 705, 638, 701) Tunnel drops and service stops while the GSA client is present and reporting Identity Intune custom compliance check + Conditional Access (require compliant device) GSA not installed, or its services not running — no event required to trigger it A failure that slips past one layer is caught by the other: If GSA stops mid-session, the firewall restricts access near real-time; If GSA is missing or disabled entirely, Conditional Access refuses the device to access Entra ID integrated resources. Under the hood: the building blocks The full solution is a set of several components, which all can be delivered and governed through Microsoft Intune: Component What it does Firewall profile Base firewall settings — default block all inbound and outbound connectivity across all profiles (public, private, and domain). Firewall rules Allow mandatory programs and services (~35 rules); restrict HTTP(S) in the Public profile using Dynamic Keywords; allow “unrestricted” HTTP(S) in the Private profile. Defender Dynamic Keywords (Reusable Settings) The set of FQDNs required for Entra ID, Defender for Endpoint, Intune, Windows Update, and Global Secure Access. Platform scripts Switch the firewall network profile to Private (unrestricted HTTP(S)); update the Defender anti-malware engine so it supports the Dynamic Keywords feature. Win32 app package Required app that deploys the scheduled tasks and the underlying PowerShell scripts. Custom device compliance check Validates that GSA is installed and checks the local GSA service state. The firewall rules that make it work The heart of the enforcement is a pair of “World Wide Web Services” outbound rules — one per firewall profile: Rule Profile Action Ports Remote destinations World Wide Web Services (HTTP & HTTPS Out) Private Allow 80, 443 Any address World Wide Web Services (HTTP & HTTPS Out) Public Allow 80, 443 Dynamic Keywords only The Private HTTP/HTTPS rule is deliberately open, because GSA is the gatekeeper. The Public HTTP/HTTPS rule scopes outbound web traffic down to the endpoint categories expressed as Dynamic Keywords: GSA Edge Endpoints, Microsoft 365 Common and Office Online, Microsoft 365 encryption chains, Windows 11, Intune & Autopilot, and Defender for Endpoint. Because these are Defender Dynamic Keywords with AutoResolve ( AutoResolve dynamic keyword addresses ) deployed via Microsoft Intune reusable settings ( Use reusable groups of settings policies in Microsoft Intune ), rather than hard-coded IP ranges, the allow-list includes endpoints centrally instead of being frozen into a brittle registry key — directly addressing the scale and maintainability limits of the old URL Lock Proxy. Besides the mentioned outbound HTTP/HTTPS firewall rule for the public and private network profile, additional rules are required for our scenario. With those additional firewall rules we cover: Basic Windows operating system network communication, Communication for Global Secure Access, and Critical Windows processes and services. Two sources did the heavy lifting: The local security event log on the device, which is essential during enrollment and reset scenarios when the profile-switching lifecycle is first established; and Microsoft Defender advanced hunting, to surface blocked connection attempts while the device is in its restricted, fail-close state. For example, this advanced hunting query surfaces outbound connections from the PAW that were blocked while it was failing closed: DeviceNetworkEvents | where DeviceName == "paw" | where LocalIPType == "Private" and RemoteIPType == "Public" | where ActionType == "ConnectionFailed" | sort by Timestamp desc Reviewing these "ConnectionFailed" events tells you whether the restricted rule set is too tight (legitimate management traffic being blocked and needing an exemption) or working exactly as intended (unexpected destinations being denied while the device is locked down). Key takeaways Global Secure Access is the right tool for controlling PAW internet access — but its currently default fail-open behavior is unacceptable for a privileged workstation. You don’t need a new GSA client to fix it. Windows Defender Firewall network profiles, driven by GSA’s own event log, give you a reliable fail-close backstop. Defender Dynamic Keywords keep the locked-down state both minimal and maintainable, replacing brittle, unscalable allow-lists. Enforcement runs at two independent layers — network (Defender Firewall profiles) and identity (Intune custom compliance plus Conditional Access) — so a failure that evades one is still caught by the other. The compliance check specifically covers the case the firewall cannot see: GSA not installed or its services not running. The whole solution deploys through Intune — Win32 app, firewall profile and rules, and a custom compliance check — and is observable through the event log and Defender advanced hunting. The Fail-Close solution turns a gap into a safe default: the instant Global Secure Access stops protecting the workstation, the privileged access workstation stops trusting the internet. We hope this article gives you a practical pattern to harden your own privileged endpoints — and if you’d like to hear more about how we design and implement our Secure Privileged Access (SPA) strategy (for instance leveraging Global Secure Access to secure on-Premises management, secure access and management of Azure private resources, what Entra ID identity controls we are using to protect privileged access, or how we leverage Identity Governance to simplify governance for privileged users), feel free to reach out to us and stay tuned for more articles. By: Christian Friedel-Jain - Sr. Security Consultant | James Noyce - Sr. Security Solution Engineer 

Introduction

Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) are among the most sensitive endpoints in any organization. A PAW, in most of our Microsoft consulting projects, exists to do one job safely: administer cloud services from a hardened device that is only ever allowed to reach a small, tightly controlled set of internet destinations. But an endpoint’s security posture is ultimately defined by its behavior under failure conditions.

When we moved the internet access restriction for our PAW devices from a locally enforced restriction (more about that later) to a solution based on Microsoft Global Secure Access (GSA), we immediately identified a gap under failure conditions – but first a quick grounding on the moving parts.

Global Secure Access (What is Global Secure Access?) is Microsoft’s umbrella term for Microsoft Entra Internet Access and Microsoft Entra Private Access — the components of Microsoft’s Security Service Edge solution. For a PAW device we are leveraging Microsoft Entra Internet Access as an identity centric secure web gateway solution to control exactly which internet destinations the workstation can reach, by applying a fine-grained set of rules and policies enforced through Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra.

This configuration provides us better filtering capabilities, like web content filtering (Global Secure Access web content filtering) with TLS inspection (TLSi) (Global Secure Access transport layer security inspection) and additional features like Threat Intelligence (Global Secure Access threat intelligence), but it comes also with a downside. Currently by default, if the GSA client encounters an issue or cannot connect to its required GSA edge services, the GSA client will fall back to a fail-open state, rather than to a fail-close state.

 

Difference between those two modes:

  • Fail-Open: When a security or control mechanism fails, access is still allowed.
  • Fail-Close: When the security or control mechanism fails, access is blocked.

 

This blog post covers above problem and showcases a solution we built, as part of our projects, to achieve a “Fail-Close” state rather than having the current “Fail-Open” behavior.

 

The enforcement of the “Fail-Close” solution we developed works at two independent layers, both are deployable through Microsoft Intune:

  • A network layer: Windows Defender Firewall network profiles, a rule set with Windows Firewall Dynamic Keywords, and event-driven automation — restricts the device internet access in the moment GSA’s tunnels or services drop.
  • An identity layer: an Intune custom compliance check paired with Conditional Access — denies the device access whenever the GSA client is missing or its services are not running.

Together, they help to make sure a failure that slips past one layer is still caught by the other.

 

 
From URL Lock Proxy to Global Secure Access

Historically, we restricted internet access on PAW devices with the Windows Defender Firewall (for more details see here Microsoft Defender Firewall) and a “URL Lock Proxy” approach (and here URL lock proxy): an allow-list of permitted URLs that blocked every outbound HTTP(S) connection except the ones required for:

  • Approved management portals,
  • Authentication to Microsoft Entra ID,
  • Management by Microsoft Intune, and
  • Monitoring by Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
 
Previous internet access control via URL lock proxy.

It worked, but it carried real limitations:

  • No auditing of what was allowed or blocked,
  • It did not scale and required a lot of wildcards to be used,
  • A limited ruleset size — the size cap on the underlying registry key meant the solution simply could not grow, and
  • It was not enterprise class.

 

Microsoft Global Secure Access with its component Entra Internet Access replaces the URL Lock Proxy configuration entirely. We are using dedicated firewall rules for the GSA client, to allow the client to reach the Entra Internet Access edge service. Through Entra Condition Access, a GSA Internet Access traffic profile (security profile) is applied which blocks all internet access except the specific FQDNs needed for approved management portals/platforms, Entra ID authentication, Intune, and Defender for Endpoint. HTTP and HTTPS traffic is evaluated and filtered within the GSA Edge service itself, and a request to a destination that is not on the allow-list is blocked with a simple “You can’t access this destination” message.

Additional features like filtering on URL level instead of FQDN, due to the use of TLSi, helped to remove most of the wildcards we had to use with the previous URL lock proxy approach.

The result is:

  • Access and the access results are auditable,
  • More granular and centrally managed rule set,
  • And genuinely enterprise class.
 
PAW internet access control via Entra Global Secure Access Internet AccessResult of blocked internet access

 

The catch: Global Secure Access fails open

GSA as the internet access restriction method is powerful, but it builds on the assumption that the GSA client is installed, running, and connected. When that assumption breaks, the client’s current behavior is to fail open.

As a result, the device ends up with unrestricted internet access whenever:

  • The GSA client is installed but cannot establish its tunnels with the GSA edge services (according to the Entra ID SLA this doesn’t happen that often – see Service Level Agreement performance for Microsoft Entra ID),
  • The GSA client on the PAW is installed but suspended, or
  • Its services are disabled, or
  • The GSA client component is not installed at all on the PAW device.
Current fail open behavior in case GSA internet access is not available

 

 

Left: normal operations - GSA internet access blocks access | Right: failure state - no filtering of internet access traffic

 

On a regular end user device, the fail-open mode is a convenience. On a PAW it is exactly the wrong default: the very moment the protection drops away, the device becomes its most exposed. Therefore, we had to develop a solution to have a fail-close behavior.

 
The Fail-Close approach

The core idea is deliberately simple, and it uses capability that already exists on most of the Windows devices: the Windows Defender Firewall network profiles (more details here Windows Firewall Network Profiles).

Two of the available firewall profiles are repurposed to act as separate operating modes:

  • Private profile: “unrestricted” HTTP(S). Internet access filtering is delegated to GSA Internet Access, so the firewall itself does not constrain destinations.
  • Public profile: “restricted” HTTP(S). Outbound web traffic is limited to a mandatory set of FQDNs via Defender Dynamic Keywords and selected system processes — just enough for the device to stay managed and healthy.

 

When the GSA client has successfully established its Internet access tunnel, the device is assigned the Private network profile. If GSA fails, the Windows Firewall profile is automatically switched to the Public network profile, restricting Internet access to essential destinations only. This profile transition implements the required fail-close behavior.

Normal state — Private profile Normal state - Windows Firewall profile "private" doesn't perform internet access restrictions, GSA internet access performs filtering

As soon as the GSA client is running, connected to the GSA edge services and has established the Internet Access tunnel (step 1), the client writes a success event to the GSA event log (step 2) (Internet Access tunnel connected — Event ID 142)

When that event occurs, a scheduled task (step 3) runs a PowerShell script (step 4) that:

  • Switches the device to the Private firewall network profile,
  • Validates the state of all local GSA services, and
  • Initiates an Intune custom compliance check (to perform additional validations).

In case all validates were successfully passed, the PowerShell script enforces the Private firewall profile (step 5) and GSA Internet Access is being used to filter the internet access (step 6).

Failure state — Public profile

 

Failure state - Windows Firewall profile "public" enforces internet access restrictions

The moment GSA stops protecting (step 1) the device, one of several failure events is written to the GSA event log (step 2) and triggers a different scheduled task (step 3) which runs a PowerShell script (step 4) that switches the device to the Public firewall network profile (step 5) and initiates an Intune custom compliance check, too. The failure signals we watch for are:

  • Entra or Internet Access tunnel disconnected — Event ID 141 (logged roughly every 10 seconds while the tunnel is down),
  • GSA services stopped — Event IDs 106, 206, 406, and 705,
  • No internet connectivity — Event ID 638, and
  • Services start initiated — Event ID 701.

 

On the Public profile, the HTTP(S) outbound rule has Reusable Settings (Defender Dynamic Keywords - Windows Firewall Dynamic Keywords) (step 6) assigned, which restricts the reachable FQDNs down to a mandatory set of endpoints. Additionally, mandatory applications and services are explicitly exempt from that restriction, so the device can still be managed, patched, and monitored even while it is locked down.

Left: normal operations - GSA internet access blocks access | Right: failure state - internet access filtering by Windows Firewall

 

Closing the gap when GSA is absent: custom compliance

The firewall profile switch is event-driven — it reacts to the signals the GSA client writes to the event log. That works well for a device where the GSA client is present, but it leaves one blind spot: if the GSA client is not installed at all, or its services never start, there may be no events to react to.

Those are exactly the scenarios where a device would otherwise fall back to unrestricted access, the solution uses a custom device compliance policy/check that does not depend on any event firing. It directly:

  • Validates that the GSA client is installed on the device, and
  • Checks the local GSA service state — confirming that the services are running, not just present.

 

If either of those checks fails — GSA client is not installed, or its services are not running — Intune reports the device as non-compliant. Because a PAW’s access to cloud resources is gated by Conditional Access requiring a compliant device, a non-compliant PAW is denied access to the very cloud services it exists to manage. So even in the one case the event-driven firewall switch cannot see, access still fails closed — this time at the identity layer rather than the network layer.

In addition, as soon as the local evaluation detected a non-compliant scenario, the custom compliance check flips the firewall profile to the Public profile, too.

The profile-switching PowerShell scripts also initiate this compliance evaluation as they run in both the normal and failure states, so the device re-reports its posture promptly instead of waiting for the next routine Intune check-in. The result is defense in depth — two independent layers, neither relying on the other:

Enforcement layer

Mechanism

What it catches

Network

Defender Firewall profile switch, driven by GSA event IDs (141, 106, 206, 406, 705, 638, 701)

Tunnel drops and service stops while the GSA client is present and reporting

Identity

GSA not installed, or its services not running — no event required to trigger it

 

A failure that slips past one layer is caught by the other:

  • If GSA stops mid-session, the firewall restricts access near real-time;
  • If GSA is missing or disabled entirely, Conditional Access refuses the device to access Entra ID integrated resources.

 

Under the hood: the building blocks

The full solution is a set of several components, which all can be delivered and governed through Microsoft Intune:

Firewall profile

Base firewall settings — default block all inbound and outbound connectivity across all profiles (public, private, and domain).

Firewall rules

Defender Dynamic Keywords (Reusable Settings)

The set of FQDNs required for Entra ID, Defender for Endpoint, Intune, Windows Update, and Global Secure Access.

Required app that deploys the scheduled tasks and the underlying PowerShell scripts.

Validates that GSA is installed and checks the local GSA service state.

The Private HTTP/HTTPS rule is deliberately open, because GSA is the gatekeeper. The Public HTTP/HTTPS rule scopes outbound web traffic down to the endpoint categories expressed as Dynamic Keywords:

  • GSA Edge Endpoints,
  • Microsoft 365 Common and Office Online,

Because these are Defender Dynamic Keywords with AutoResolve (AutoResolve dynamic keyword addresses) deployed via Microsoft Intune reusable settings (Use reusable groups of settings policies in Microsoft Intune), rather than hard-coded IP ranges, the allow-list includes endpoints centrally instead of being frozen into a brittle registry key — directly addressing the scale and maintainability limits of the old URL Lock Proxy.

Microsoft Intune Reusable Settings

As mentioned in the section before, several endpoint categories are being used as part of the Public "World Wide Web Services (HTTP & HTTPS Out)" Firewall rule. As part of this blog post, we cannot publish a one-size fits all list of FQDNs, since the actual list of FQDNs highly depends on the actual configuration, scenario or environment and are subject to change (as usual when it comes to endpoints). In our scenario it was important that PAW devices, when not connected to GSA, are able to:

  • Perform authentication against Microsoft Entra ID,
  • Remains fully managed by the MDM, in our case Microsoft Intune,
  • Receive updates for the operating system (Windows 11 Enterprise) and the XDR solution (Defender for Endpoint), and
  • Are able to connect to Microsoft Global Secure Access edge services.

Based on the requirements we leveraged several publicly available endpoint lists, which include the following, to create our Reusable Settings configuration:

  • GSA Edge Endpoints - FQDN and IP addresses where the Global Secure Access service receives traffic
  • Microsoft 365 - Microsoft 365 URLs and IP address ranges
  • Windows 11 - Connection endpoints for Windows 11 Enterprise
  • Intune & Autopilot - Network endpoints for Microsoft Intune
  • Defender for Endpoint - Microsoft Defender for Endpoint streamlined connectivity URLs
Create Reusable Settings objects

Attached to this blog post you will find several CSV files (GlobalSecureAccessEdgeEndpoints.csv, DefenderforEndpoint.csv, IntuneAutopilot.csv, Microsoft365Common.csv, Microsoft365encryptionchains.csv, Windows11.csv) which include the lists of FQDNs we are using as part of our deployments.

Disclaimer: We are sharing those Reusable Settings lists with you AS IS without warranty. Keep in mind that the config might require modifications to match to your scenario or environment.

 

The following code example can be used to create the Reusable Settings Object in Intune via Graph API. The code example doesn't include any error handling, since it should give you an idea how to perform the import, based on a CV file.

 

Code example for Reusable Settings import via CSV:

$csvFile = Get-Item 'C:\temp\GlobalSecureAccessEdgeEndpoints.csv' $definitionId = 'vendor_msft_firewall_mdmstore_dynamickeywords_addresses_{id}' $values = Import-Csv -LiteralPath $csvFile.FullName | ForEach-Object { $row = $_ $autoResolve = [bool]::Parse($row.AutoResolve) $autoResolveValue = $autoResolve.ToString().ToLowerInvariant() $choiceChildren = if (-not $autoResolve) { @{ '@odata.type' = '#microsoft.graph.deviceManagementConfigurationSimpleSettingCollectionInstance' settingDefinitionId = "${definitionId}_addresses" settingInstanceTemplateReference = $null simpleSettingCollectionValue = @( $row.Addresses -split ';' | Where-Object { -not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($_) } | ForEach-Object { @{ '@odata.type' = '#microsoft.graph.deviceManagementConfigurationStringSettingValue' settingValueTemplateReference = $null value = $_.Trim() } } ) } } @{ '@odata.type' = '#microsoft.graph.deviceManagementConfigurationGroupSettingValue' settingValueTemplateReference = $null children = @( @{ '@odata.type' = '#microsoft.graph.deviceManagementConfigurationSimpleSettingInstance' settingDefinitionId = "${definitionId}_id" settingInstanceTemplateReference = $null simpleSettingValue = @{ '@odata.type' = '#microsoft.graph.deviceManagementConfigurationStringSettingValue' settingValueTemplateReference = $null value = "{$([guid]::NewGuid())}" } } @{ '@odata.type' = '#microsoft.graph.deviceManagementConfigurationChoiceSettingInstance' settingDefinitionId = "${definitionId}_autoresolve" settingInstanceTemplateReference = $null choiceSettingValue = @{ '@odata.type' = '#microsoft.graph.deviceManagementConfigurationChoiceSettingValue' settingValueTemplateReference = $null value = "${definitionId}_autoresolve_$autoResolveValue" children = @($choiceChildren) } } @{ '#microsoft.graph.deviceManagementConfigurationGroupSettingCollectionInstance' settingDefinitionId = $definitionId settingInstanceTemplateReference = $null groupSettingCollectionValue = @($values) } } Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementConfiguration.ReadWrite.All' Invoke-MgGraphRequest ` -Method POST ` -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/reusablePolicySettings' ` -Body ($body | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20) ` -ContentType 'application/json'

 

Important: A maximum of 100 properties can be stored in a single reusable settings group object. Therefore, it might be required to split a endpoint category into multiple Reusable Settings Group objects.
Intune Win32 app package

Besides the deployment of the actual Global Secure Access client, a dedicated application package will be used to deploy the local components (Scheduled Tasks and PowerShell scripts) for the fail-close approach. To react on the two different states (normal and failure), two Scheduled Tasks need to be deployed to the PAW device. The Scheduled Task creation can be simplified by using exported XML files, which can also include the event trigger itself (examples listed in the sections Normal State and Failure State). Please note, the creation of Scheduled Tasks with event log based triggers require that the actual event log already exists on the device. So it might be worth creating a dependency between the different application packages.

 

Example code to register exported Scheduled Tasks via PowerShell:

Register-ScheduledTask -Xml (Get-Content "$PSScriptRoot\GSA-Connected.xml" | Out-String) -TaskName 'GSA-Connected' Register-ScheduledTask -Xml (Get-Content "$PSScriptRoot\GSA-Disconnected.xml" | Out-String) -TaskName 'GSA-Disconnected'

 

XML Sample Scheduled Task export GSA-Connected:

Sample XML Scheduled Task export GSA-Disconnected:

2026-09-10T17:46:11.8914414 ChristianFriedel-Jain \GSA-Disconnected true *[System[(EventID=141)]] and *[EventData[Data[@Name='Channel Name'] and (Data='Entra')]] true *[System[(EventID=141)]] and *[EventData[Data[@Name='Channel Name'] and (Data='Internet')]] true *[System[Provider[@Name='Microsoft-Windows-Global Secure Access Client'] and EventID=106]] true *[System[Provider[@Name='Microsoft-Windows-Global Secure Access Client'] and EventID=206]] true *[System[Provider[@Name='Microsoft-Windows-Global Secure Access Client'] and EventID=406]] true *[System[Provider[@Name='Microsoft-Windows-Global Secure Access Client'] and EventID=705]] true *[System[Provider[@Name='Microsoft-Windows-Global Secure Access Client'] and EventID=638]] true *[System[Provider[@Name='Microsoft-Windows-Global Secure Access Client'] and EventID=701]] S-1-5-18 HighestAvailable IgnoreNew false false true false false true false true true false false false true false PT1H 7 "C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe" -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "C:\Progra~1\GSA-NetDetection\Set-NetworkPublic.ps1"

 

As soon as one of the Scheduled Tasks has been triggered, the corresponding PowerShell script (Set-NetworkPrivate.ps1 or Set-NetworkPublic.ps1) will be executed.

Example content of Set-NetworkPrivate.ps1 (updated 2026-10-13)

$NetworkName = (Get-NetConnectionProfile).Name $GSAServices = @( "GlobalSecureAccessClientManagerService" "GlobalSecureAccessEngineService" "GlobalSecureAccessForwardingProfileService" "GlobalSecureAccessTunnelingService" ) $GSAServicesRunning = 0 foreach ($service in $GSAServices) { if ((Get-Service -Name $Service -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Status -eq "Running") { $GSAServicesRunning += 1 } else { $GSAServicesRunning += 0 } } if ($GSAServices.Count -eq $GSAServicesRunning) { Set-NetConnectionProfile -Name $NetworkName -NetworkCategory Private } else { Set-NetConnectionProfile -Name $NetworkName -NetworkCategory Public Start-Process -FilePath "C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Intune Management Extension\Microsoft.Management.Services.IntuneWindowsAgent.exe" -ArgumentList "intunemanagementextension://synccompliance" }

Example content of Set-NetworkPublic.ps1 (updated 2026-10-13)

$NetworkName = (Get-NetConnectionProfile).Name Set-NetConnectionProfile -Name $NetworkName -NetworkCategory Public Start-Process -FilePath "C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Intune Management Extension\Microsoft.Management.Services.IntuneWindowsAgent.exe" -ArgumentList "intunemanagementextension://synccompliance"

 

Platform scripts Install Microsoft Defender Antivirus updates during the device enrollment

To leverage the AutoResolve dynamic keyword feature, Microsoft Defender Antivirus must be turned on and running with platform version 4.18.2209.7 or later (see reference here FQDN Feature requirements). Since the required version is not natively included in Windows yet, a Platform script is being used to install the required Defender updates (Use the command line to manage Microsoft Defender Antivirus)

Example command to trigger Defender update:

$MpCmdRun = "C:\Program Files\Windows Defender\MpCmdRun.exe" & $MpCmdRun -SignatureUpdate -MMPC

 

Switch Defender Firewall profile to private during enrollment phase

To avoid issues during the device enrollment phase, the Defender Firewall profile is being switched from the default Public profile to the unrestricted Private profile by using another Platform Script.

Example code to switched the Firewall profile:

$NetworkName = (Get-NetConnectionProfile).Name Set-NetConnectionProfile -Name $NetworkName -NetworkCategory Private

 

Custom device compliance check

A custom device compliance check is being used to validate if GSA is installed and if the services are running on the device. A custom device compliance check requires an underlying script to gather the required information.

Example custom compliance script:

# GSA services to check $Services = @( "GlobalSecureAccessClientManagerService" "GlobalSecureAccessEngineService" "GlobalSecureAccessForwardingProfileService" "GlobalSecureAccessTunnelingService" ) $GSAInstalled = $false $RunningGSAServices = 0 # Validate that all Services are present (GSA installed) if ((Get-Service $Services[0] -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) -and (Get-Service $Services[1] -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) -and (Get-Service $Services[2] -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) -and (Get-Service $Services[3] -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) { $GSAInstalled = $true } else { $GSAInstalled = $false } # Validate Service State foreach ($Service in $Services) { if ((Get-Service -Name $Service -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Status -eq 'Running' ) { # Service running - increase number of running services by 1 $RunningGSAServices += 1 } else { # Service not running - will not increase number of running services $RunningGSAServices += 0 } } if (($RunningGSAServices -ne 4) -or ($GSAInstalled -eq $false)) { Set-NetConnectionProfile -NetworkCategory Public } # Create a hashtable with the collected data $hash = @{ "GSAinstalled" = $GSAInstalled "GSArunning" = $RunningGSAServices } return $hash | ConvertTo-Json -Compress

 

The result of the custom compliance script will be evaluated against the custom compliance policy, which requires the custom compliance settings in a JSON format.

Example custom compliance settings JSON:

{ "Rules": [ { "SettingName": "GSAinstalled", "Operator": "IsEquals", "DataType": "Boolean", "Operand": "true", "MoreInfoUrl": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/global-secure-access/overview-what-is-global-secure-access", "RemediationStrings": [ { "Language": "en_US", "Title": "Global Secure Access not detected", "Description": "Global Secure Access service not found on the device." } ] }, { "SettingName": "GSArunning", "Operator": "IsEquals", "DataType": "Int64", "Operand": "4", "MoreInfoUrl": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/global-secure-access/overview-what-is-global-secure-access", "RemediationStrings": [ { "Language": "en_US", "Title": "Global Secure Access services not running", "Description": "One or more Global Secure Access service is not running on the device." } ] } ] }

 

Validating and monitoring

How did we work out which rules and events mattered — and how do we confirm the solution keeps working? Two sources did the heavy lifting:

  • The local security event log on the device, which is essential during enrollment and reset scenarios when the profile-switching lifecycle is first established; and
  • Microsoft Defender advanced hunting, to surface blocked connection attempts while the device is in its restricted, fail-close state.

 

For example, this advanced hunting query surfaces outbound connections from the PAW that were blocked while it was failing closed:

DeviceNetworkEvents | where DeviceName == "paw" | where LocalIPType == "Private" and RemoteIPType == "Public" | where ActionType == "ConnectionFailed" | sort by Timestamp desc

 

Reviewing these "ConnectionFailed" events tells you whether the restricted rule set is too tight (legitimate management traffic being blocked and needing an exemption) or working exactly as intended (unexpected destinations being denied while the device is locked down).

 

Key takeaways
  • Global Secure Access is the right tool for controlling PAW internet access — but its currently default fail-open behavior is unacceptable for a privileged workstation.
  • You don’t need a new GSA client to fix it. Windows Defender Firewall network profiles, driven by GSA’s own event log, give you a reliable fail-close backstop.
  • Defender Dynamic Keywords keep the locked-down state both minimal and maintainable, replacing brittle, unscalable allow-lists.
  • Enforcement runs at two independent layers — network (Defender Firewall profiles) and identity (Intune custom compliance plus Conditional Access) — so a failure that evades one is still caught by the other. The compliance check specifically covers the case the firewall cannot see: GSA not installed or its services not running.
  • The whole solution deploys through Intune — Win32 app, firewall profile and rules, and a custom compliance check — and is observable through the event log and Defender advanced hunting.

 

The Fail-Close solution turns a gap into a safe default: the instant Global Secure Access stops protecting the workstation, the privileged access workstation stops trusting the internet.

 

We hope this article gives you a practical pattern to harden your own privileged endpoints — and if you’d like to hear more about how we design and implement our Secure Privileged Access (SPA) strategy (for instance leveraging Global Secure Access to secure on-Premises management, secure access and management of Azure private resources, what Entra ID identity controls we are using to protect privileged access, or how we leverage Identity Governance to simplify governance for privileged users), feel free to reach out to us and stay tuned for more articles.

items.title: NHS England evolves its cybersecurity strategy with Palo Alto Networks and IBM
items.summary: The NHS has set an ambitious goal of achieving cyber resilience across healthcare organisations by 2030. Delivering on that vision requires technology, expertise and close collaboration across the public and private sectors. This is clearly a highly complex task, but one we're delighted to help deliver in partnership with IBM. Through this partnership, Palo Alto Networks will provide advanced cloud-based perimeter technology, alongside IBM Consulting’s specialist guidance, implementation support and tailored onboarding for NHS organisations. As health and care services continue to modernise, maintaining resilient, secure digital infrastructure has never been more important. Healthcare organisations are operating in an increasingly complex environment, with growing digital dependencies, expanding supply chains, evolving cyber threats and new technologies such as AI reshaping the landscape. According to IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report , healthcare continues to be one of the most impacted sectors globally when it comes to the financial consequences of cyber incidents. This highlights the importance of taking a proactive, long-term approach to cyber resilience across critical public services. Palo Alto Networks' continued work with the NHS demonstrates the scale and complexity of securing modern healthcare environments. As organisations balance innovation, operational demands and evolving security requirements, there is a growing need for solutions that provide both strong protection and the flexibility to meet local needs. Introducing the Next Generation of the NHS Secure Boundary Programme Palo Alto Networks will deliver next-generation, cloud-based security solutions through the next iteration of the NHS Secure Boundary programme. The service has been designed to help strengthen cyber resilience across UK health and social care organisations while supporting the safe and reliable delivery of services. Secure Boundary provides the capability to support a network spanning more than 1.5 million NHS staff, over 200 NHS trusts, more than 55,000 organisations handling health data and approximately 2 million devices under national cyber monitoring. The nationally integrated and centrally funded service embodies a "Defend as One" approach, helping organisations benefit from shared protection while retaining local control. Secure Boundary supports NHS organisations through: An AI-enabled cybersecurity capability designed to strengthen resilience and support the safe, reliable delivery of healthcare services. Enhanced visibility and protection for internet traffic across the Health and Social Care Network. Improved security for infrastructure and clinical applications operating across multiple service providers. Increased protection for information shared across NHS organisations and trusted third parties. Greater privacy and security for staff accessing web-based services, whether on-site or remotely. A "Defend as One" approach that complements existing local security measures while allowing organisations to tailor policies to their specific requirements. Reduced complexity through the consolidation of security tools and management processes. Improved efficiency through a centrally funded model that helps reduce duplication of technology and investment. The new Secure Boundary service represents a significant step forward in strengthening the NHS's digital resilience. By providing a more secure foundation for NHS services, it helps support operational continuity, safeguard sensitive information and enable healthcare teams to continue delivering high-quality care in communities across the UK for years to come. If you would like to find out more about Secure Boundary and how it can help your organisation, please contact ukpubsec@paloaltonetworks.com .
